notes:
Task and constraints: Find the lowest common ancestor of two existing nodes p and q in a binary search tree.
Idea: While root exists, move to root.left if both values are smaller, move root.right if both are larger, and otherwise return root as the split point or one of the targets.
Technique and why it applies: BST ordering directs the search toward both targets until their paths diverge.
Invariant: Both p and q remain in the subtree rooted at root.
Edge cases: If one target is root, root is returned; targets on opposite sides meet at root; a missing path would fall out with None although inputs promise existing nodes.
Complexity: Time O(h), space O(1).
complexity_reason: Each iteration descends one child link, visiting at most h nodes.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the lowest common ancestor of two existing nodes in a BST.
Idea: Iterate while root is non-null; go left when both p.val and q.val are smaller, go right when both are larger, and return root otherwise.
Technique and why it applies: The BST's sorted ordering identifies a common branch until the values straddle the root or equal it.
Invariant: The subtree rooted at root still contains both requested nodes.
Edge cases: If p or q equals root, root is returned; targets in separate branches return their split node; null root returns null. Comparisons use int node values.
Complexity: Time O(h), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop follows at most one child pointer per tree level and stores no stack.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the lowest common ancestor of two existing nodes in an arbitrary binary tree, with no BST ordering to guide search.
Idea: Return root if null or identical to p/q; recursively search left and right, return root when both results are nonempty, otherwise propagate the nonempty result.
Technique and why it applies: Postorder recursion combines evidence from both subtrees to find the first node whose branches contain the two targets.
Invariant: Each recursive result is a target found below that node or the LCA of both targets.
Edge cases: If root is p or q, it returns immediately; targets in separate subtrees make root the LCA; a leaf unrelated to either returns None.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(h).
complexity_reason: Each node is visited at most once and recursion depth follows tree height.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the lowest common ancestor of two existing nodes in a general binary tree.
Idea: Stop at null, p, or q; recurse into both children, return root when both results are non-null, otherwise return whichever result exists.
Technique and why it applies: Recursive postorder aggregation detects the point where searches for p and q meet.
Invariant: A non-null return means the subtree contains one target or already contains the lowest common ancestor.
Edge cases: Root equal to p returns root; targets in separate branches return their common parent; a missing target may cause the method to propagate only the found node, but the statement promises both exist.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(h).
complexity_reason: The recursion visits each node at most once and uses one call frame per level.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return each element's product excluding itself without division.
Idea: Fill out with ones, store the product of values before i in out[i] during a forward pass, then multiply by the running suffix product in a backward pass.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix and suffix products combine all values except nums[i] without needing division, so zeros are handled naturally.
Invariant: Before the backward pass updates i, out[i] is the product left of i and suffix is the product right of i.
Edge cases: [1,2,3,4] becomes [24,12,8,6]; one element yields [1]; zeros correctly zero products only where included.
Complexity: Time O(n), O(1) extra space excluding output.
complexity_reason: Two passes visit n elements and keep only prefix and suffix scalars beyond out.

notes:
Task and constraints: Build a product-except-self array without division.
Idea: In the forward loop write each prefix product into out[i], then scan backward multiplying each entry by suffix and updating suffix with nums[i].
Technique and why it applies: Separate prefix and suffix accumulators form each output from values on both sides, including arrays containing zero.
Invariant: During the backward pass, out[i] holds the left product before suffix is applied, and suffix contains the product to the right.
Edge cases: [1,2,3,4] yields [24,12,8,6]; a singleton produces [1]; int multiplication may overflow if product constraints exceed Java int range.
Complexity: Time O(n), O(1) auxiliary space excluding output.
complexity_reason: The two loops each traverse the array once and maintain one scalar product.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the maximum of every contiguous window of size k in nums.
Idea: Remove indices outside the window from dq's front, remove indices whose values are no greater than the new value from the back, append i, and emit nums[dq[0]] once a full window exists.
Technique and why it applies: A decreasing deque of candidate indices discards values that can never be maximum while preserving the best eligible index.
Invariant: dq indices increase, their values decrease, and the front is the current window maximum.
Edge cases: k=1 emits each value; decreasing input keeps many candidates; equal values discard the older index because the newer one expires later.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(k).
complexity_reason: Each index is appended once and removed at most once from either end of dq.

notes:
Task and constraints: Compute sliding-window maxima for an array and valid window size k.
Idea: Maintain deque indices, evict expired front indices, pop weaker values from the back, append i, and write the front value into out after the first full window.
Technique and why it applies: The monotonic deque keeps only indices that can still become a future window maximum.
Invariant: Deque indices are increasing and corresponding nums values strictly decrease after removing <= values.
Edge cases: k=1 returns the original values; equal values favor the later index; output allocation assumes 1<=k<=nums.length or its length may be invalid.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(k).
complexity_reason: Every index enters and exits the deque at most once, and out stores n-k+1 results.

notes:
Task and constraints: Search target in a matrix sorted ascending across each row and each column.
Idea: Start at the top-right cell; if value is too large move left, if too small move down, and return true on equality.
Technique and why it applies: At the top-right corner, each comparison eliminates a full row or column that cannot contain target.
Invariant: If target remains, it lies in the rectangle from row r downward and column 0 through c.
Edge cases: Empty matrix or empty first row returns false; a match at the starting corner succeeds; target below all values eventually moves beyond the last row.
Complexity: Time O(m+n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: Each step decreases c or increases r, so there are at most m+n moves.

notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether target occurs in a row-and-column sorted int matrix.
Idea: Return false for empty dimensions, begin at top-right, then decrement c for values above target or increment r for values below it.
Technique and why it applies: Sorted rows and columns make each corner comparison discard one whole row or column.
Invariant: The remaining candidate rectangle is bounded by rows r onward and columns up to c.
Edge cases: Empty dimensions return false; equality returns true immediately; the loop ends when r reaches row count or c becomes negative. Rectangular shape is assumed.
Complexity: Time O(m+n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The row index only increases and the column index only decreases, limiting steps to m+n.

notes:
Task and constraints: Decide whether s and t contain the same characters with the same multiplicities.
Idea: Construct Counter(s) and Counter(t) and compare the two frequency mappings.
Technique and why it applies: Character-frequency equality is exactly the multiset condition for anagrams and ignores character order.
Invariant: Each Counter records the number of occurrences of every character in its string.
Edge cases: Empty strings are anagrams; 'listen' and 'silent' compare true; strings with different counts or lengths compare false. Python supports arbitrary Unicode characters, not only lowercase English.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(u) for distinct characters (O(1) under a fixed alphabet).
complexity_reason: Counter scans both strings and stores one count per distinct character.

notes:
Task and constraints: Check whether two lowercase English strings are anagrams.
Idea: Reject unequal lengths, increment counts for s.charAt(i), decrement counts for t.charAt(i), then require all 26 counters to be zero.
Technique and why it applies: Paired frequency updates cancel matching character multisets regardless of order.
Invariant: After each position, counts represent the frequency difference between the processed prefixes of s and t.
Edge cases: Empty strings return true; 'listen' and 'silent' pass; unequal lengths return false immediately. Indexing char-'a' assumes lowercase English letters as specified.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop processes each character pair and the final pass checks a fixed 26-element array.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the missing number from n distinct values in [0,n], with one value absent.
Idea: Initialize result to len(nums), then XOR each index and nums value into result; return the remaining bit pattern.
Technique and why it applies: XOR cancels every index/value pair that appears twice, leaving the missing value.
Invariant: result is the XOR of n, all processed indices, and all processed array values.
Edge cases: [3,0,1] returns 2; a list containing 0 through n-1 returns n; empty nums returns 0.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop visits each array entry once and keeps one XOR accumulator.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the absent integer from the distinct range 0..n represented by an array of length n.
Idea: Seed result with nums.length, then XOR it with each index and corresponding nums[i].
Technique and why it applies: XOR is self-cancelling, so all present values and their matching indices vanish while the missing value remains.
Invariant: result equals the XOR of the initial n and every processed index/value pair.
Edge cases: [3,0,1] returns 2; missing n leaves result n; empty array returns 0. Java int bitwise XOR operates on all 32 bits without arithmetic addition overflow.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The for loop performs two XOR operations per element and stores one integer result.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the duplicate among n+1 values in [1,n] without modifying nums.
Idea: Binary-search candidate values from 1 to len(nums)-1; count entries <=mid and keep the lower half when count exceeds mid, otherwise advance lo.
Technique and why it applies: The pigeonhole count test identifies a value range containing more entries than distinct values, so that range must contain the duplicate.
Invariant: The duplicate remains inside [lo,hi].
Edge cases: [1,3,4,2,2] returns 2; duplicate at n is retained by upper bounds; nums is never modified.
Complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: Each binary-search round scans n values to count entries <=mid, and the range halves.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the repeated value in n+1 integers from 1 to n without modifying the input.
Idea: Binary-search values; count how many nums entries are <=mid, set hi=mid if count>mid, otherwise lo=mid+1.
Technique and why it applies: More than mid values in [1,mid] proves a duplicate in that range by the pigeonhole principle.
Invariant: The duplicate remains between lo and hi after every count-based decision.
Edge cases: [1,3,4,2,2] returns 2; the array is never reordered; mid uses lo+(hi-lo)/2 to avoid index-sum overflow.
Complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: Each search iteration scans the array once and the candidate interval shrinks logarithmically.

notes:
Task and constraints: Maintain a stream and return its median after any number of insertions.
Idea: Store lower values as negatives in max-heap lower and upper values in min-heap upper; addNum inserts then swaps tops and rebalances sizes, while findMedian uses one or both roots.
Technique and why it applies: Two heaps partition values around the median and keep the middle elements accessible at their roots.
Invariant: lower has either equal size to upper or one extra element, and every lower value is <= every upper value.
Edge cases: One number is its own median; two values average their roots; Python / returns a float for even counts. Empty findMedian is not guarded.
Complexity: add O(log n), median O(1), space O(n).
complexity_reason: Each insertion performs a constant number of heap operations and the heaps store all stream values.

notes:
Task and constraints: Support integer insertions and median queries over a growing stream.
Idea: lower is a reverse-order PriorityQueue and upper is a min-heap; addNum inserts into lower, transfers roots to restore order and size, and findMedian returns the top or average.
Technique and why it applies: Two heaps maintain the lower and upper halves while exposing the central value(s).
Invariant: lower has the same size as upper or one extra, and lower.peek() is no greater than upper.peek().
Edge cases: A single item is its median; two items average both roots; casting lower.peek() to long prevents int overflow when adding extreme values. Empty queries are not guarded.
Complexity: Insertion O(log n), median O(1), space O(n).
complexity_reason: Each insertion performs a bounded number of heap offers/polls and both heaps retain all inserted values.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence, not necessarily contiguous.
Idea: For each value use bisect_left(tails,value); append if it exceeds every tail, otherwise replace the first tail that is >= value.
Technique and why it applies: Patience-sorting tails maintain the smallest possible ending value for each subsequence length, enabling binary search updates.
Invariant: tails is sorted and tails[j] is a minimal tail for an increasing subsequence of length j+1.
Edge cases: Empty nums returns 0; [10,9,2,5,3,7,101,18] returns 4; equal values replace rather than extend because the subsequence is strictly increasing.
Complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n).
complexity_reason: The loop processes n values and each bisect_left searches the tails list logarithmically.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the length of a strictly increasing subsequence in nums.
Idea: Binary-search tails[0:size] for the first entry >= value, replace that slot, and increase size only when the insertion position equals size.
Technique and why it applies: The tails array stores minimal endpoints by subsequence length, and binary search updates those endpoints in logarithmic time.
Invariant: tails remains sorted and tails[j] represents the smallest known endpoint for a subsequence of length j+1.
Edge cases: Empty input returns 0; duplicates replace an existing tail rather than extending size; the sample LIS length is 4. The fixed array has nums.length capacity.
Complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n).
complexity_reason: For each element the binary search touches O(log n) tails entries and the array stores at most n tails.
